common_name: Lufkin Mayhaw (East Texas Western Mayhaw Selection)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown trees in late winter to early spring in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun near a creek bottom or low spot that mimics its natural wet-footed habitat.

directions: Lufkin is a named selection of western mayhaw grown and propagated in the East Texas pineywoods region and recognized in Texas mayhaw-growing circles alongside other named selections such as Big V and Super Spur. Like other western mayhaws, it tolerates seasonally wet, poorly drained bottomland soil far better than most fruit trees and produces heavy clusters of tart red, cherry-sized fruit in late spring that are prized for mayhaw jelly. Plant it with a second mayhaw cultivar nearby to improve fruit set, and expect some susceptibility to fire blight and cedar rust common to the genus. Full sun and consistent moisture during fruit development give the best yields.

common_name: Juhl American Persimmon (Kansas Native Persimmon Selection)

planting.note: Plant grafted bare-root or container trees in late winter to early spring in full sun in moist, well-drained soil, siting them away from foot traffic since the deep taproot resents transplant disturbance.

directions: Juhl is a selection of the native American persimmon found in southeastern Kansas, long circulated among fruit-tree hobbyists and nut-tree nurseries for its productive bearing and relatively few seeds per fruit. As with most American persimmon cultivars, fruit must fully ripen and soften after frost before eating, since unripe fruit is intensely astringent from tannins. Give it a sunny, well-drained site and pair it with a genetically distinct seedling or cultivar if consistent pollination is a concern, as American persimmons can vary in their need for a pollinator depending on the individual tree's flower type. Established trees are tough, drought-tolerant once rooted in, and need little maintenance beyond occasional removal of root suckers.
sources: Kansas State University Research and Extension

common_name: Miner Plum (Historic Midwest Native American Plum)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or grafted stock while still dormant in late winter to early spring in well-drained soil in full sun; pair with a second American plum for reliable fruit set.

directions: Miner is one of the oldest and most widely planted named selections of American plum, dating to 19th-century Midwest orchards and long valued as a reliable, cold-hardy producer of tart, thick-skinned red fruit used mainly for jams, jellies, and preserves. It is not self-fruitful, so plant it with a second American plum seedling or cultivar nearby to ensure cross-pollination and a useful crop. Like other native plums, it tolerates drought, poor soil, and harsh winters far better than introduced plum species, but it suckers from the root and benefits from occasional thinning to control spread. Site it in full sun on well-drained ground for the healthiest growth and best fruiting.
sources: USDA Bureau of Plant Industry historical plum variety records
Iowa State University Extension and Outreach

common_name: Cheney Plum (Historic Upper Midwest Native American Plum)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or grafted stock while still dormant in late winter to early spring in well-drained soil in full sun; cross-pollination with a second American plum is required for fruit set.

directions: Cheney is a historic American plum selection from the upper Midwest, documented in early 20th-century pomology surveys and later used as breeding stock for several cold-hardy hybrid plums developed at northern land-grant universities. It bears clusters of medium, red-skinned, yellow-fleshed fruit in late summer, useful fresh or cooked down for preserves. As with other American plums, it is not self-fruitful and needs a second, genetically distinct plum nearby to cross-pollinate and set a crop. The tree is exceptionally cold- and drought-tolerant compared to introduced plum species, tolerates poor soil, and suckers readily from the root, so remove unwanted suckers to keep it in bounds.
sources: Iowa State University Extension and Outreach
American Pomological Society historical fruit catalog records
